top_choice_rationale: P004 (Grossman and Helpman, B013) has the cleanest attribution on the slate, a stable two-person partnership with jointly authored core papers, and about three decades of maturity. Its achievement is specific: protection became an equilibrium outcome of lobbying and electoral incentives. The framework produced sharp, estimable predictions and organised later empirical work on tariff structures and trade agreements. It is also the trade-policy strand, where overlap with the 2008 prize is weakest. The main discount is the mixed empirical record of the specific Protection for Sale predictions. I weigh that against the framework's influence and judge the case sufficient for a prize. P001 (Autor, Hanson, Dorn on a narrow citation) is a close second. It has a credible design, a decade of replication and now converged attribution, but its magnitudes are debated and it sits near recent prizes. P005 is third because the Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum claims cannot be honoured in the Melitz-Helpman attribution. P002 follows because its empirical content is indirect, and P003 because it is still maturing and depends on restricted data. A prize this year is preferable to none, so P000 is last.
recusal_note: No connection to Grossman, Helpman, Melitz, Autor, Dorn, Hanson, Rubinstein, Wolinsky, Chetty, Hendren or Friedman is apparent from the profile. My political-economy-of-growth work is thematically adjacent to P004, which is field proximity only. Long-term co-author Violante is credited on B004, which is not on the slate. I frequently co-author with Hassler (chair, supporter of P005) and Boppart (supporter of P001) and am their IIES colleague. This is disclosed and not adjudicated.
